extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, political reformers, and students of representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles for structuring executive power, the judiciary, the civil service, and local representative bodies in a free government; guidance on appointments, removals, electoral franchise, and local constituencies. Aimed at informing constitutional and administrative design to preserve freedom and effective administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive ability to dissolve Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: The head of the administration should have the power to dissolve the House and appeal to the people; instead of being turned out of office by a hostile vote, he could be reduced by it to the alternative of resignation or dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power prevents deadlock between executive and legislature, avoids prolonged mutual paralysis (which could invite coups), and provides a constitutional means to test which party has the stronger following; it is desirable even if the executive holds office for a fixed period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deadlock between president and assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought not to be any possibility of that deadlock in politics which would ensue on a quarrel breaking out between a president and an assembly, neither of whom, during an interval which might amount to years, would have any legal means of ridding itself of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems must provide mechanisms (e.g., dissolution) to prevent prolonged stalemate that could lead to coups or paralysis; relying solely on mutual forbearance and compromise is imprudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary power to remove a dangerous first magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the vast power centralized in the chief magistrate, and the insufficient attachment of the mass of the people to free institutions, give him a chance of success in an attempt to subvert the Constitution, no first magistrate is admissible whom the Parliament can not, by a single vote, reduce to a private station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is real peril of usurpation, constitutional dependence of the executive on Parliament (ability to remove by single vote) is required as safeguard; otherwise even strong dependence may be a weak protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges should not be popularly elected
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all officers of government, those in whose appointment any participation of popular suffrage is the most objectionable are judicial officers. Popular election is ill-suited to assess the special and professional qualifications of judges and undermines impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular elections would subject judges to appeals to public opinion and passion, encourage politicization of judicial decisions, and make judges consider popularity rather than justice; judicial responsibility to executive or popular vote has been shown to pervert conduct more than irremovability (except for serious misconduct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of judges only for proved and serious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: It is far from desirable that there should be no means of getting rid of a bad or incompetent judge, unless for such misconduct as he can be made to answer for in a criminal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While irremovability has evils, the peculiar position of judges means that removal should be constrained to serious culpability to protect judicial independence; popular removal threatens impartiality and fair adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation in justice via juries, not judge elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The participation of the general public in the administration of justice is of the greatest importance; but in what manner? By the actual discharge of a part of the judicial office in the capacity of jurymen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct public involvement is valuable as jurors who hear cases with necessary precautions and impartiality; this is preferable to exposing judges to popular opinion through elections or recalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive public examinations for first appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: All candidates for first appointments should be submitted to a public examination, conducted by persons not engaged in politics, and of the same class and quality with the examiners for honors at the Universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public, impartial competitive examinations minimize partiality and private/political interest in first appointments and give the best chance of honest and meritocratic appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examinations must be competitive and appointments to top performers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is absolutely necessary that the examinations should be competitive, and the appointments given to those who are most successful. A mere pass examination never, in the long run, does more than exclude absolute dunces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive ranking stimulates effort, raises educational standards, produces incentives across educational institutions, and prevents gradual lowering of proficiency that follows lenient pass-exams or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination content should test general mental cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain whether a candidate has been well educated, he must be interrogated in the things which he is likely to know if he has been well educated (e.g., classics and mathematics), even though not directly pertinent to the work to which he is to be appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad tests of mental cultivation are justified because general education is useful; objections that test questions are irrelevant misunderstand that some questions are meant to distinguish high proficiency and are not required of all candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsequent promotion by mixed seniority and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the first admission to government employment be decided by competitive examination, subsequent promotion should take place on a mixed system of seniority and selection: routine duties by seniority and special-trust functions by selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for high-trust roles should be made by office chiefs and will be honest if original appointments were by open competition; seniority suits routine progression while selection rewards special capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local affairs should be handled by local representative bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indispensable to share duties between central and local authorities. The popular control over local officers can only be advantageously exerted through a separate organ; representative sub-Parliaments for local affairs are fundamental institutions of a free government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central authorities should not busy themselves with local matters; local representation enables better management, division of labor, and public education of citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local institutions as instruments of public education
rubrics_metrics.description: Local administrative institutions are the chief instrument of the public education of the citizens: acting in local office gives many citizens the chance to think, speak, and act for public interests rather than merely thinking through proxy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local offices provide practical political education, bring lower social grades into contact with higher minds, and cultivate political intelligence more effectively than national politics which is mostly thinking without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local franchise should include those contributing to local rates
rubrics_metrics.description: As the principal duty of the local bodies consists of the imposition and expenditure of local taxation, the electoral franchise should vest in all who contribute to the local rates, to the exclusion of all who do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franchise should reflect direct local fiscal responsibility; representation of minorities should follow the same principles as national representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural voting and money qualification more defensible locally
rubrics_metrics.description: There are strong reasons for plurality of votes; in the inferior as in the higher body there is not so decisive an objection to making the plural voting depend on a mere money qualification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because frugal and honest dispensation of money forms larger part of local business, allowing greater proportional influence to those with larger money interest is more justifiable in local elections than nationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit ex officio membership and include educated class where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In Boards of Guardians the justices of peace sit ex officio along with elected members, in number limited by law to a third of the whole, which secures the presence of a more educated class without allowing dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited ex officio presence can check lower-class interests and raise the caliber of local bodies; by contrast, bodies composed solely of justices (e.g., Quarter Sessions) are excessively aristocratic and at variance with representative government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local constituencies by community of local interests
rubrics_metrics.description: In local circumscription, community of local interests is the only just and applicable principle. Every town ought to have its municipal council, and every town ought to have but one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local representation should group inhabitants who share the same local needs (paving, lighting, water, drainage, markets); subdividing a single town into multiple independent districts impedes unified administration and wastes resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: One elective body for all local business (unified control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In each local circumscription there should be but one elective body for all local business, not different bodies for different parts of it. The executive duties may be departmentalized, but control should be united.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single superintending body can oversee all departments more effectively than many minute separate elective bodies; unity of control attracts higher-calibre members and prevents degeneration into self-interest and jobbing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include some of the best local minds; avoid tiny municipal councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Local bodies should contain a portion of the very best minds of the locality to bring superior contact to inferior minds; a mere village has no claim to a municipal representation and is better merged into a larger circumscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small places often lack a sufficient public for a tolerable council and risk domination by one person; larger circumscription and inclusion of prominent minds improves local administration and political education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local circumscription tailored to type of local business
rubrics_metrics.description: Local representation of rural districts will naturally be determined by geographical considerations, with due regard to sympathies of feeling that follow historical boundaries and community of interest (agricultural, maritime, manufacturing, or mining districts). Different kinds of local business require different areas of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design boundaries according to shared local interests and the nature of the services to be provided rather than arbitrary size; ensure areas fit the practical needs of the particular local functions.
